content.title: How the Shock of 9/11 Makes Flying Safer
content.lead: Since the 2001 terrorist attack, further attacks involving airplanes have been prevented. Various changes on the ground and on board contributed to this. The question, however, is whether this success will endure.
content.author: Andreas Spaeth

image.author: Spencer Platt / Getty
image.caption: Following the attacks of September 11, 2001, many airlines installed bulletproof cockpit doors to prevent terrorists from boarding. The image shows JetBlue chief pilot Lanny McAndrews with the new security door.
image.altText: 396032 01: Chief pilot of JetBlue Airways Lanny McAndrew, stands behind one of the new bullet-force-resistant cockpit doors that have been installed on all JetBlue planes after the September 11 attacks, October 17, 2001 at JFK airport in the New York borough of Queens. The reinforced cockpit doors, which cost the company approximately $10,000 per aircraft, are the first such doors to be installed on a major carrier. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

content.caption: Following the attacks of September 11, 2001, many airlines installed bulletproof cockpit doors to prevent terrorists from boarding. The image shows JetBlue chief pilot Lanny McAndrews with the new security door.
content.author: Spencer Platt / Getty

content.text: Twenty-five years ago, more than half of the nineteen terrorists who hijacked four airplanes and used them as weapons were initially stopped at security checkpoints. However, after a brief secondary inspection, all were permitted to pass and board their flights, despite carrying items such as sharp box cutters.

How could this happen? This occurred despite the devastating findings of a 1990 investigation conducted by a U.S. presidential commission after the catastrophic bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland. Eleven years prior to the September 11, 2001 attacks, the commission concluded: «The security system of American civil aviation shows serious weaknesses and has failed to offer the necessary protection to the traveling public. It needs fundamental reform; rhetoric is no substitute for strong, decisive measures.»

image.author: Bob Riha Jr / Getty
image.caption: After the 9/11 attacks, baggage screening at airports became significantly stricter and more comprehensive.
image.altText: International travelers wait and line up for security clearance by United States Customs and Immigration Officers at Los Angeles International Airport, January 3, 1990 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images)

content.caption: After the 9/11 attacks, baggage screening at airports became significantly stricter and more comprehensive.
content.author: Bob Riha Jr / Getty

content.text: Back then, much was considered normal that is difficult to fathom today: only about five percent (compared to one hundred percent today) of checked baggage was inspected for explosives. In the U.S., anyone could proceed to the gates after checking in at the checkpoint – even without a flight ticket. In Scandinavian countries, there were often no security checks at all on domestic flights. And pilots in the cockpit worldwide were separated from the cabin only by thin folding doors. These served primarily as privacy screens and often remained open during flights.

content.teaserCaption: The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, changed America and the world. How do they continue to shape geopolitics and the global economy today?
content.leadText: The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, changed America and the world. How do they continue to shape geopolitics and the global economy today?

content.text: After September 11, 2001, significant changes occurred regarding aviation security. Aviation security, in English, refers to the prevention of interference with air traffic.

The list of measures from the last two decades is long, and the U.S. was consistently a pioneer: by 2003, all cockpit doors worldwide had to be massively reinforced and equipped with an access system. Additionally, the U.S. was the first to arm pilots, beginning in 2003. Following foiled attacks, such as that by the «shoe bomber,» a rule requiring the removal of shoes during screening was implemented in the U.S. from 2006.

Flight security officers, the so-called Air Marshals of the newly formed Transportation Security Administration (TSA), soon began their service, from 2006, also on flights aboard American aircraft departing from Europe. In the same year, restrictions on liquids in carry-on luggage took effect, and in 2008, full screening of all checked baggage was introduced. Beginning in 2010, passengers were screened by full-body scanners, and since 2018, their carry-on luggage has been processed by new CT scanners. Typically, unpacking is no longer required. Liquids are also once again permitted in many locations.

image.author: Seth McAllister / EPA
image.caption: In 2001, security measures at airports and on airplanes were still lax. This was the only reason terrorists were able to fly two planes into the towers of the World Trade Center.
image.altText: This September 11, 2001 file photo shows the second hijacked airliner, United Airlines Flight 175 from Boston, Massachusetts, approaching the south tower of the World Trade Center as the north tower burns in the forground after it was impacted by American Airlines Flight 11, also out of Boston. EPA PHOTO AFPI/SETH MCALLISTER/EH/DEC/fm/rlb/ac

content.caption: In 2001, security measures at airports and on airplanes were still lax. This was the only reason terrorists were able to fly two planes into the towers of the World Trade Center.
content.author: Seth McAllister / EPA

content.text: «Technology-driven improvements such as CT scanners and better data exchange have proven much more effective than crude methods akin to security theater – such as the compulsion to remove shoes,» says Samuel Ramani, who advises the governments of Great Britain and the U.S. on geopolitical risks for a London-based think tank.

«Thanks to new CT scanners, the rule about removing shoes could be lifted,» Ramani says. He illustrates that smarter technology can replace outdated rituals – with the same or even higher security levels. However, he warns that terrorists are also constantly upgrading, for example with 3D-printed weapons or new chemical explosives.

«It will be crucial to understand technological developments early, continuously reassess risks, and accordingly further develop existing protection concepts,» Swiss said in response to an NZZ inquiry.

image.author: Claudio Thoma / Keystone
image.caption: A newly installed system with full-body scanners today facilitates security checks at Zurich Airport.
image.altText: A newly installed security scanner in the security control building (SCB) at Zurich Airport. This building, equipped with new CT scanners, security scanners, and centralized remote screening systems, was photographed before its commissioning on Friday, December 5, 2025, at Zurich Airport in Kloten. (KEYSTONE/Claudio Thoma)

content.caption: A newly installed system with full-body scanners today facilitates security checks at Zurich Airport.
content.author: Claudio Thoma / Keystone

content.text: Increased security also meant significant adjustments for crews, as Thomas Steffen, airline captain and media spokesperson for the pilots' association Aeropers, confirms: «The most drastic rule was probably that the cockpit door must be closed whenever possible.» This complicated cooperation with the cabin crew and interaction with passengers, the Aeropers spokesperson adds.

Among Swiss airlines and pilots, there is consensus: «For security, the cockpit door rule and door reinforcement were the most important,» Steffen notes. He adds that developments in passenger and cargo screening also had an immense share in the improvement seen today.

Swiss also experienced significant changes. The significantly tightened requirements for identity verification and passenger screening (so-called «passenger vetting») had been particularly formative for previously valid security procedures, the Swiss airline stated. This also included the consistent securing of the cockpit and additional security requirements for flights to the U.S.

image.author: Claudio Thoma / Keystone
image.caption: Thanks to CT scanners, baggage can be inspected more easily for suspicious items today – comprehensively at Zurich Airport from summer 2026 onwards.
image.altText: A police officer demonstrates a 3D model of a tray at the newly installed CT scanner for passenger and staff hand luggage in the new security screening building (SKG) at Zurich Airport. Equipped with new CT scanners, security scanners, and centralized remote screening systems, the building was photographed before its commissioning on Friday, December 5, 2025, at Zurich Airport in Kloten. (KEYSTONE/Claudio Thoma)

content.caption: Thanks to CT scanners, baggage can be inspected more easily for suspicious items today – comprehensively at Zurich Airport from summer 2026 onwards.
content.author: Claudio Thoma / Keystone

content.text: «The fact that an event like 9/11 has not been repeated in the past 25 years is an indication that the international security architecture works,» a Swiss spokesperson emphasizes. However, individual measures alone have not been decisive, but rather the entirety of the package of measures, he adds.

On some flights by Swiss airlines, flight security officers continue to accompany. «For us, Inflight Security Officers are a clear asset for air traffic security,» Thomas Steffen of the pilots' association Aeropers emphasizes. They have since become a normal part of aviation, he adds.

content.text: «The multifaceted measures after 9/11 demonstrably had a positive impact on security. In this area, civil aviation has made immense progress in the last 25 years,» Steffen summarizes.

The Swiss aviation security expert and historian Jonathan Zimmerli, who previously worked for both United Airlines and various Swiss authorities in the field, also says: «Personally, I feel very safe when I fly. The attention to fending off possible attacks on air traffic is very high today.»

The focus today is on new and future dangers. «Cyber threats are not just a future concern for aviation but are already intensely occupying it today,» Swiss explained. Artificial intelligence, the airline added, is likely to act in both directions: it can create new risks, but at the same time also offer new opportunities to recognize risks earlier and further improve security.

However, aviation remains a prominent target for external attacks, a Swiss spokesperson says. «Today we have a very comprehensive and multi-layered security system. At the same time, we must not rest on this success,» the spokesperson adds. It is important to recognize new threats early and continuously develop the security architecture, he notes. Passengers should report anything unusual, «when in doubt, it is better to report something too often than not often enough,» he advises.

The expert Jonathan Zimmerli also emphasizes that humans remain a decisive factor in preventing dangers: «Even with today's AI-supported security technologies, one must not forget the human element. One must also invest there and provide good training for employees, deploying them equipped with human insight.»

newestTopComments.text: According to this text, the most modern scanner version has been in use since 2018. It's been operational at Zurich Airport since this summer. Why? Every other airport worldwide is significantly more advanced than Zurich. They act as if Kloten (Zurich Airport) is the center of the universe and Swiss the best airline in the world. Far from it! In recent weeks, Swiss flights have had to make emergency landings, turn back, etc., practically every week. What's going on? Are they unreliable, not rigorous enough in enforcing the rules, which, after all, have to apply to everyone on board, or what? Not good publicity for Swiss. And once again, they're saying that security checks are taking longer at the airport because of new EU regulations. Why can't they just implement innovations quickly and efficiently, like other airports do?
